# Statistics theory and code

What the model is doing, in enough detail to defend it in review, and then the
same analysis run end to end on published data you can download.

::: {.callout-warning}
Draft. The section structure below is fixed and matches the class; the prose is
being written.

Every `##` section gets its own figure, as in Chapter 1. One H2 is one slide, so
the figure is also that slide's visual, and a section without one leaves the
deck with a blank.
:::

Theory first, then the code that fits it. The two were separate classes until
2026-10-20; they are one now, because nobody defends a model they have not run
and nobody trusts a fit they cannot explain. The code sections follow the same
order as the theory, so each fit lands next to the reason for it.

## The problem: correlated estimates within a study

Why estimates sharing one reference group cannot be treated as independent, and
what goes wrong when they are.

## Reconstructing the within-study covariance

The Greenland and Longnecker result [@greenland1992], and the refinements by
study design [@orsini2006].

## Two-stage estimation

Fit a trend in each study, then pool the trends. The practical reference is
@orsini2012.

## One-stage estimation

A single linear mixed model across all studies, which keeps studies that
two-stage drops [@crippa2019].

## Choosing a functional form

Linear, quadratic, restricted cubic splines. Where to put knots and why the
default is defensible but not sacred.

## Heterogeneity in a dose-response model

What heterogeneity means when the thing varying is a curve rather than a number.

## Alternatives worth knowing

Robust error meta-regression [@xu2018], Bayesian formulations [@hamza2021], and
when each is the better answer.

## The worked example

What the physical activity review asked, and why it is a good first dataset.

## Getting the data into shape

The extraction sheet as an R data frame, and the viability check before fitting.

## Fitting a linear dose-response model

The simplest defensible fit, with `dosresmeta` [@dosresmeta].

## Fitting a spline model

Restricted cubic splines, knot placement, and comparing fit against the linear
model.

## Plotting the curve

Building the figure that will carry the paper, with the confidence band and the
observed exposure range marked.

## Naming the shape

Using the fit's own `curve_label` so the results paragraph and the figure agree.

## Sensitivity analyses in code

Varying knots, dropping influential studies, and switching to one-stage.
